children: By Gertrude Chavez-Dreyfuss

US Treasuries rebounded on Tuesday after a sharp selloff in the previous session pushed long-term yields to multi-decade highs, as investors paused to assess recent moves ahead of next week's inflation data, which could offer fresh clues on where interest rates are headed.
A solid three-year auction also added to Treasuries' bullish momentum.
In afternoon trading, the benchmark 10-year yield fell 4.2 basis points to 5.269%
after scaling a 24-year peak on Monday. US 30-year yields slid 2.2 bps to 5.642% (US30YT=RR) following Monday's 24-year high.
On the shorter end of the curve, US 2-year yields, which are sensitive to the outlook for interest rates, were down 4.4 bps at 4.789% (US2YT=RR). Falling yields mean Treasury prices are higher.
"I think traders are catching their breath before anything changes with the fundamentals," said Will Compernolle, macro strategist at FHN Financial in Chicago.

"They are also waiting to see what the next big catalyst will be and I don't know if that's going to be PPI (producer prices) or CPI (consumer prices). But yields are already elevated and I think before they rise any further, traders need to see a ... more convincing reason for yields to continue cheapening."
Analysts also said US Treasuries found support after a similar rally in eurozone bonds, particularly those from
, with their yields declining as well.
France's borrowing costs have surged in recent weeks and the yield gap over

expanded to its widest since the euro zone debt crisis in 2011 last Friday. The jump in yield came amid worries about the country's deteriorating fiscal situation ahead of next year's presidential election.

Elsewhere in the Treasury market, the yield curve flattened on Tuesday, with the spread between two-year and 10-year yields narrowing to 47.8 bps from 48.9 late Monday. The curve had reached its steepest level in seven weeks on Monday after long-dated yields rose more sharply than shorter-dated ones, a move known as a bear steepener.
REVERSING RECENT STEEPENING

Analysts said Tuesday's flattening largely reflected a reversal of earlier steepening pressures amid renewed focus on persistent inflation risks, rising government borrowing needs, and concerns over the US fiscal outlook.
Those concerns, some investors argued, have yet to be fully reflected in Treasury prices.

Olivier d'Assier, senior director of investment decision research at SimCorp in Singapore, said it was still too early to turn positive on Treasuries despite the recent bond market selloff. SimCorp is a global provider of investment management software and services.

"Clearly there's a crisis going on and there isn't a credible solution being offered. Most governments especially the US government are not even pretending to try to balance the budget," d'Assier said.
"So if you want to lend money to someone and they're telling you they're going to keep spending more than they earn, you will think twice before lending."

For now, however, those concerns have not translated into weaker demand for US government debt. Tuesday's three-year note auction drew decent demand, pricing at 4.932%, below the expected yield at the bid deadline. The yield was above than the six-auction average of 4.167%.

The bid-to-cover ratio, another indication of investor appetite, was slightly soft at 2.62 times, compared with an average of 2.65 times in the last six auctions. Direct bidders took  31.7% of supply, the largest since February.
Direct participants refer to those institutions or individuals that submit bids directly to the US Treasury for their own portfolios rather than on behalf of third party clients.

US 3-year yields have risen by 48 bp since the last sale in September and JPMorgan said in a research note that the 3-year debt is fairly valued after adjusting for the level of rates and the shape of the curve over the last three to six months.
